title: Akamonkai vs ISI: Two Very Different Approaches to Japanese Study
summary: One school splits its purposes across campuses, the other splits them across programmes in one place. That structural difference decides more than any ranking.
body_html:
These two get compared on size and reputation, which tells you almost nothing. The difference that matters is structural, and it is visible in how each one organises itself.

ISI separates purposes by campus. Akamonkai separates them by programme inside one school. Everything practical follows from that.

ISI: the campus you attend is chosen by your goal

ISI's Tokyo campuses include Shinjuku main, Shinjuku Prime, Ikebukuro, Takadanobaba Academic, Takadanobaba Career and Shibuya-Harajuku Career. [source:1] It also operates outside Tokyo, in Osaka, Kyoto and Nagano. [source:1]

Look at those names. Takadanobaba appears twice — once as an academic campus, once as a career campus. Shibuya-Harajuku is a career campus. The purpose is in the campus name because the purpose is what the campus is.

The course list matches: an academic Japanese course, a Japanese career course, short intensive and short career options, and an evening course. [source:1]

What that means for you: deciding between university preparation and job hunting is not a timetable choice at ISI, it is a decision about which building you walk into every morning — and therefore about your commute, your neighbourhood and who your classmates are.

It also means the city is a real option. If you would rather study in Kyoto or Nagano than Tokyo, that exists here. [source:1] That is unusual and worth something if a quieter place suits how you learn.

The flip side is less obvious. If your goal changes — and plenty of students arrive planning university and leave planning to work — changing track may mean changing campus.

Akamonkai: one school, programmes layered inside it

Akamonkai runs a general study-abroad course, a preparatory education course, a business employment class, a premium employment support option, a named corporate ICT employment programme, and semi-regular and short courses. [source:2]

Same purposes, organised the other way. You enrol in the school and then sit in the programme that fits, and if your plan changes you are changing class rather than address.

Two of its programmes have no direct equivalent in ISI's published list.

The preparatory education course. This is designated by the Ministry of Education for people whose secondary education runs to fewer than 12 years, so that they qualify for Japanese university entry. [source:2] It runs 1 year 6 months or 2 years. [source:2]

This is not a teaching-style preference. It is an eligibility fix. If your country's schooling stops short of that, this course is what makes Japanese university possible for you, and a school without one cannot substitute for it however good its Japanese teaching is.

A named corporate employment programme. Akamonkai lists an ICT employment programme carrying a specific company's name. [source:2] We are not going to characterise what that gets you — the school has not published outcomes for it that we could verify — but a programme built around one company's technology stack is a different proposition from general job-hunting support, and worth asking about directly if that industry is your target.

The employment numbers, and how to read them

Akamonkai publishes figures for employment, and they are a good illustration of why headline rates need their denominator.

The school states that more than 90 percent of students in its business employment class secure work with Japanese companies each year. [source:3]

Notice which population that is. It is the business employment class — a specific programme people opt into — not the school. A rate for a self-selected cohort that chose an employment track answers a different question from a rate across everyone.

For the general study-abroad course, the school reports employment results as a count instead: 211 students in total for the 2025 academic year. [source:3] A count and a rate are not comparable, and the school has not published the denominator that would make them comparable.

None of this suggests anything is being hidden — the page is clear about which programme each figure belongs to. The point is for you: if you are comparing this against a number from another school, check you are comparing the same population. Most of the time you are not.

Which one suits which person

  • Fewer than 12 years of secondary schooling. [source:2] Akamonkai, for the designated preparatory course. This is an eligibility question, not a preference.
  • Clear single goal, already decided. ISI — a campus built for that purpose, with classmates who are all there for the same thing. [source:1]
  • Goal still moving. Akamonkai — switching programmes does not mean switching campus. [source:2]
  • Want to live outside Tokyo. ISI, which operates in Osaka, Kyoto and Nagano. [source:1]
  • Targeting employment in ICT specifically. Ask Akamonkai about the named corporate programme, and ask what the outcomes have actually been. [source:2]
  • Want a short trial before committing. Both publish short-course options — ISI short intensive and short career courses, Akamonkai semi-regular and short courses. [source:1] [source:2] Ask which are actually running, because short courses come and go.

Questions to put to both

Neither school publishes what you most need to know, so ask:

  • How many parallel classes run at my level in the intake I am applying for? This decides whether placement fits you or approximately fits you.
  • If my goal changes after six months, what actually happens — new class, new campus, or wait for the next intake?
  • For any employment or progression figure quoted at me: which students are in the denominator, and which year?
  • What is the current fee schedule for my intake, in writing?

Our profiles list what each publishes: Akamonkai and ISI. ISI's published fee structure is broken down in what the ISI total actually includes. If dormitories matter to your decision, Akamonkai runs its own — see the schools that provide dormitories.

Course lists, campuses and figures change by academic year, and the schools' own pages linked below are the authority. We prepare and forward application documents; admission is decided by the school and tuition is paid directly to it.

claims_without_sources: 両校の教学水準・指導の質の優劣 —— 比較できる客観指標がない。構造（校区で分けるか、プログラムで分けるか）の違いだけを述べ、どちらが優れているとは書いていない。SERP では第三者が「赤門会は進学寄り、ISI は総合」と評しているが、第三者評は出典にしない。
ISI 各校区の定員・学費 —— 本記事では触れていない。学費は別記事（isi-tuition）で出典付きで扱っており、ここで重複して数字を持ち出す必要がない。
ISI に準備教育課程に相当するコースがあるかどうか —— 公開されているコース一覧には見当たらないが、「一覧に無い」ことは「存在しない」ことの証明ではない。本文では「ISI の公表コース一覧に直接の相当物がない」と書き、存在しないと断定していない。
HUAWEI-ICT 就職プログラムの実績・内容 —— 学校はプログラム名を掲げているが、成果の数値を公表していない。「何が得られるか」は書かず、直接聞けとした。企業名そのものも本文では出していない（特定企業との関係を本サイトが保証しているような含意を避けるため）。
「90％以上」の分母 —— 学校はビジネス就職クラスの受講生であることを明記しているが、受講生数そのものは公表していない。したがって率は率として引き、分母が未公表であることを明記した。
一般留学コース 211 名の分母（在籍者数）—— 公表されていない。率に換算していない。

「3週間体験コース」—— コース一覧ページの HTML に文字列は存在するが、2 箇所ともすべて HTML コメント（<!-- -->）の中にあり、表示されるページには出ていない。学校が掲載を取り下げたと読むのが自然で、現に提供されているコースとして書くべきではない。闸门は strip_tags でコメントを落とすため「ページ上に無い」と判定した —— これは正しい挙動で、取り下げられたコースを現役として書くのを防いだ。
「中等教育が11年の国」という具体例 —— 出典は「12年未満」とだけ書いており、11 という数字はこちらの例示。闸门が未標記の数字として弾いたのが正しく、数字を落として「それに届かない場合」と書き換えた。
